ACT-SC6-P1-Q1.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous. I decoded Figure 1 from the SVG independently (y=132 is 0 min, y=22 is 50 min, so value=(132-y)/2.2) and then rendered the SVG at 680/340/300/260 px and looked at it. The Additive M point at 5 mg/L is an open diamond centred at y=96.8 -> exactly 16 min, sitting just above the unlabelled 15-min minor tick (y=99). Minor ticks at 5/15/25/35/45 are present and resolvable, so 16 is readable as 'just above 15', and the only competing option (21) sits just above the 20-min major gridline, ~11 px away. No tick, marker or label gave me trouble. Curve identity is also safe: the letters J/K/L/M are printed at the right-hand end of each curve, 3 px below its final marker, and the four endpoints are 85.8/66/52.8/41.8 - at least 11 px apart - so tracing the dash-dot/open-diamond series back to 5 mg/L is not a coin toss. CROSS-ITEM: no. The four options here are exactly the four curves' values at 5 mg/L, so nothing is decidable without the figure; a no-source solver sees four bare times. One small note for the set as a whole: this key (16 min) reappears as a distractor in Q5, and Q5's 12 min distractor is the control level that Q6 turns on, so a student who works the passage in order gets mild elimination help on Q5. Benign, but it is the only cross-item channel I found.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q2.pick: Additive J gave its greatest clearing time of the concentrations tested
ACT-SC6-P1-Q2.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous, but this is the second-tightest read in the batch and I checked it with my eyes rather than only with arithmetic. Experiment 2 fixed 10 mg/L (passage, not stem - that is the intended step). At 10 mg/L: J=44 (its maximum; J runs 12/30/44/36/21), K=27 (K is still climbing, max 30 at 20), L=8 (its MINIMUM), M=40 (M peaks at 42 at 15). So only J. The option that could in principle be defended is M, because M at 10 (40) vs M at 15 (42) is only 4.4 SVG px apart. I cropped that region of the 340 px render at 6x: the dash-dot line visibly ascends out of the 10 mg/L diamond and the 15 mg/L diamond sits about one marker-height higher, so 'M is at its greatest at 10' is refutable from the drawing. It is resolvable but it is not generous - if this figure is ever re-rendered smaller than ~260 px wide, re-check that gap. K and L are not close calls. Stem wording is a little laboured ('at that concentration:' + four options each repeating 'gave its greatest clearing time of the concentrations tested'), but it is not ambiguous. Note that 'of the concentrations tested' resolves to J whether or not you count the 0 mg/L control point. CROSS-ITEM: no; the option set names all four additives with identical predicates, so no option is preferable blind.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q3.note: FIGURE READ: the KEY is readable, but this is the one item where the drawing is close to its limit, and the author should see the measurement. Figure 2 scale: y=234 is 0 min, y=174 is 50 min (1.2 px per min), with gridlines ONLY at 0/25/50 - no minor ticks. Bar values decode exactly: J 44/17, K 27/29, L 8/7, M 40/36. Only K rises. I then measured the actual rendered pixels rather than trusting the numbers. At 340 px wide the K pair's bar tops are at rows 196 (unstirred) and 193 (stirred) - a clear 3-row step UP, and I can see it at 1x. It survives downscaling: 2 rows at 300 px and at 260 px. So the key is visible. The L pair is NOT: at 340 px the filled bar's top edge is row 218 and the open bar's stroke straddles rows 218-219, i.e. the pair renders as a TIE, and the intended 8-vs-7 min difference is simply not recoverable from the drawing at display size (1 min = ~1.2 px here). I still vote exclusive=true, because to defend 'Additive L' a student needs stirred STRICTLY GREATER and the pair reads level-or-lower, never higher - at 300 and 260 px the open bar is 1 px lower, which is the correct direction. But two things follow. (a) Q3's explanation asserts 'for Additive L it falls from 8 min to 7 min'; no student can see that, and if this item is ever reviewed on the strength of that sentence, the sentence is doing work the figure does not do. (b) There is a systematic drawing asymmetry: the unstirred bars are pure fill with no stroke while the stirred bars carry stroke-width 1, which extends ~0.5 px ABOVE the true top. Every open bar is therefore drawn a half-pixel tall, always in the direction of the key here. The key's true margin is +2 min and the render shows ~+2.5 min of it. That is not wrong, but the item is effectively a two-way K-vs-L discrimination decided at 2-3 px, which is why I rated the distractors only 'plausible' - J and M are dead weight (a 27 min and a 4 min fall are obvious), so three of the four options do no work. If you want this to be a real easy item rather than a near-tie, widen the K pair (e.g. 27 -> 32) and give Figure 2 minor ticks every 5 min; both would also make the L pair honest. CROSS-ITEM: no. Q3 and Q6 are the two 'name the additive' items and their keys differ (K, L), and the key sits in slot A in both - see the batch-level note on Q6.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q4.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous in both figures. Step 1 is a Figure 2 comparison that is not close: J falls 44 -> 17 (27 min, a 32 px collapse that is obvious at any render width) while K is +2, L is -1, M is -4, so 'by far more than any other' picks out J with no measurement needed - the small-margin problem that afflicts Q3 does not reach this item. Step 2 reads the solid/filled-circle J curve at 15 mg/L: marker centre y=52.8 -> exactly 36 min, one minor tick (35) below the 40 gridline, with the nearest other series (M, 42) 13 px above and K (29) 15 px below. No tick or marker was hard to resolve. Hard rather than medium because it is a four-part chain - read four bar pairs, compute four differences, carry the winning series across to the other figure, then read a value - and because the stem never names the additive. This is the best-built item in the set: each distractor is the 15 mg/L value of a DIFFERENT curve and each corresponds to a named, realistic wrong route (42 = tallest bars instead of largest drop; 29 = the additive that went up; 18 = the additive with the shortest bars). CROSS-ITEM: no. Note only that J is also the answer to Q2, but by a different property (max in Fig 1 vs largest stirring drop in Fig 2), so knowing one does not give the other.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q5.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous. The Additive K (dashed, open square) markers at 5 and 10 mg/L are at y=85.8 and y=72.6 -> 21 and 27 min, both landing just above a labelled gridline and a minor tick respectively, and the segment between them is a straight rising line, so the midpoint at 7.5 mg/L is 24 min. Nothing in the drawing resisted me here. Exclusive: the only rival is 21, and it is only reachable by refusing to interpolate at all; even a student who reads the segment as slightly concave (K flattens after 10) cannot get closer to 21 than to 24, since the true midpoint is 24.0 and the options step by 3-5 min. 'Most likely closest to' is the right hedge for an interpolation item. Distractors are the canonical error set for this skill: 21 = snap to the nearer plotted point, 16 = right x, wrong curve (M at 5), 12 = the additive-free level at the left edge. CROSS-ITEM: no, though see the Q1 note - 16 min is Q1's key, so a student who has already established that 16 belongs to M at 5 mg/L can eliminate it here without looking. Mild, and it cuts the option set to three at worst.

ACT-SC6-P1-Q6.note: FIGURE READ: unambiguous, and the baseline is the thing to check. The additive-free mean is the single open circle at 0 mg/L, y=105.6 -> 12 min, and all four polylines originate from that one point. L is the only curve that ever goes below it: 9 min at 5 mg/L and 8 min at 10 mg/L, both plotted a clear 7-9 px below the 12 min level and below the 10 min gridline, so the dip is visible at 1x. J, K and M never drop below 12 (their minima are 21, 21 and 16), so exactly one option contradicts the claim. I also checked that the item does not depend on the graphic's caption: the passage itself says the control mean 'is plotted at 0 mg/L', so if the caption is ever dropped from the render the item still stands (the same is true for Q1/Q3 - the curve letters and the unstirred/stirred legend are drawn inside the SVG, not only in the caption). Medium rather than hard, against my instinct: the stem carries the heaviest verbal load in the batch (a negated claim that you must contradict) but the visual is a giveaway - L is the ONLY curve in Figure 1 that descends at all, so a student who does not parse the logic at all can still land on it by noticing which line goes down. That tension is worth knowing: the item is rated by its stem and solved by its picture. Distractors are good because the natural wrong move - comparing curves to each other rather than to the 12 min control - makes M (lowest of the three at 16) genuinely attractive. BATCH-LEVEL ANSWER: I checked whether the six keys are guessable from the pattern across items and found no usable tell. Key slots run B, D, A, D, C, A (2 A, 1 B, 1 C, 2 D - no slot dominance, no ABCD-permutation structure). Answer additives run M, J, K, J, (K), L - no additive repeats in the two 'name the additive' items. In the three numeric items the key's rank among the four options is 2nd-smallest, 3rd, then largest, so there is no length, magnitude or extremeness tell, and every numeric option set is exactly the four curves' values at the relevant x, which means a solver without the figure faces four interchangeable times. The one structural regularity is that Q3 and Q6, the two additive-naming items, both put the key in slot A; with n=2 that is noise, but if more items of this shape are added to the passage, keep an eye on it.
